headline: Execution Rocks fires as 50-pound bass crash the Western Sound on outgoing water
subhead: Trolling Mojos over the ledges producing oversized stripers while water temps hit perfect 68-degree mark.
body_markdown:
The Western Sound is absolutely on fire right now, and I'm talking about the kind of fishing that makes you forget about everything else in the world. We've got 50-pound bass prowling the ledges, water temps sitting in that sweet spot around 68 degrees, and the kind of moving water that gets these fish feeding like they mean it.

The story of the week happened right at Execution Rocks, where the ledge structure is holding bass that'll make your arms ache. I watched one angler boat what had to be a 50-pound fish — her first striper ever, if you can believe that. But that's what happens when you're in the right place with the right presentation when these giants are feeding.

The pattern is clear as day: trolling large Mojos over the ledge structure on the outgoing tide. Morning starts slow, but when that water starts moving in the afternoon, it's lights out. I'm seeing consistent 40-inch-plus fish coming over the rails, and these aren't your typical schoolies. These are the fish we wait all season for.

The key is reading the water movement. When you've got that outgoing tide ripping over Execution Rocks, it creates an upwelling that pushes bait right into the strike zone. The bass know this, and they position themselves along that ledge drop waiting for an easy meal. Your Mojo needs to be running deep enough to tick that structure — that's when you get the violent strikes that'll test your drag.

Water temperature is sitting right at 68 degrees across most of the Sound, and that's creating a perfect thermal layer for bait to stack up. The bunker are finally showing in decent numbers, though not the massive schools we usually see this time of year. But what's there is quality — adult fish that are drawing the attention of these oversized bass.

The Stepping Stones area is producing similar results, especially on the flood tide when bait gets pushed through that channel. I'm seeing guys working bucktails with success, but you need to match the current speed. When it's ripping, go heavy — 3/4 to 1 ounce — and work it slow and steady. The bass are sitting just off the bottom waiting for something that looks like it's struggling in the current.

Matinecock Point has been consistent for slot fish, with the grass beds holding plenty of bait. Early morning topwater action has been sporadic but explosive when it happens. Pencil poppers and spooks are getting crushed when you find the right school, but you need to be there at first light when the water's still got that glassy look.

The bluefish are finally showing some size — we're talking about fish that'll actually bend your rod instead of those cocktail blues that have been plaguing us. They're mixed in with the bass schools, so don't be surprised if your Mojo gets hammered by a 5-pound blue instead of the bass you're targeting.

Fluke fishing has been steady but not spectacular. The 30-foot contour from Oyster Bay to Lloyd's Neck is holding fish, but you're working for them. White Gulp on chartreuse bucktails is the go-to rig, and you need to fish it slow on the drift. The fish are there, but they're not aggressive — you need to put the bait right in their face.

Porgies are starting to show up around the rocky structure, which is always a good sign. When the porgies move in, it means the bottom is alive with crabs and worms, and that draws everything else up the food chain. Simple high-low rigs with clam or worm are producing steady action for anyone looking to put some dinner in the cooler.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon coming Friday, which means big tides and moving water. That's exactly what we want for these big bass. The spring tides will flush more bait out of the harbors and create the kind of current that gets these fish feeding aggressively. I'll be watching the sunset bite closely — when you combine new moon darkness with that evening outgoing tide, magic happens on the Western Sound.

The water's clean, the bait's around, and the fish are feeding. This is what we've been waiting for all season. Get out there and get on them before the summer heat pushes these fish deeper or further east. The Western Sound is serving up the kind of fishing that makes legends, and right now, the window is wide open.
